stages.label: Absent
stages.desc: Nothing of the kind exists, and a dated source says so.

stages.label: Preparing
stages.desc: Announced, drafted, piloted: an intention with an instrument or a pilot behind it.

stages.label: Establishing
stages.desc: In service, but limited in scope, coverage or use.

stages.label: Operating
stages.desc: In service at scale: funded, regulated, used, maintained.

stages.label: Leading
stages.desc: Embedded: interoperable, measured, sustained; at or beyond the continental norm.

grey.label: No evidence
grey.desc: Not staged: nothing held, or evidence held that meets no rung.

gov.legislate--cybersecurity-legislation.label: Cybersecurity legislation: cybercrime and cybersecurity law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no cybercrime or cybersecurity law and no bill for one.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity bill is drafted, before parliament or passed. No law is known to be in force.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code. No use of it is on record in the past three years.
The law has been used in the past three years: a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty from the body it sets up. Who it was used against is not judged.
The law is used, and a count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under it is published for a period ending within the past two years.
A source from the past three years says the country has no data protection authority, and no law in force names one.
A law names a data protection authority. No source says its head or members have been appointed.
The authority's head or members are appointed, or an existing body given the job is doing it. No ruling against a named organisation is on record in the past three years.
The authority has ruled against a named organisation in the past three years: a decision, fine or order. A court's judgment does not count.
The authority publishes a count of its decisions, fines or complaints settled, for a period of a quarter or more ending within the past two years.
A dated source states that the country has no general data protection law, and none is on record as enacted or in preparation.
A data protection law is announced, being drafted, before parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated.
A data protection law is enacted or in force, whether it stands alone or is part of a larger law. No decision under it is on record in the past three years.

The law is in force and has been applied: a dated sanction, order, decision or court judgment on a controller within the past three years. Without a constituted supervisory authority the stage is capped at 3.
The law has regulations in force under it, and a count of decisions, sanctions or complaints settled is published for a period ending within the past two years.

gov.protect--national-data-protection-re.label: National data protection readiness: data protection system

ladder.text: No data protection law is in force: there is none, or it is still a bill or has not yet commenced.
A data protection law is in force. The country has not ratified the Malabo Convention and no authority is appointed.
A law is in force, and the country has ratified the Malabo Convention or appointed an authority. Nothing in the past three years shows the authority at work.
The law is being implemented: in the past three years an appointed authority has registered organisations, taken breach reports, issued guidance or inspected.
The authority is acting: in the past three years it has ruled against a named organisation, or it publishes a count of its rulings. A court's judgment does not count.
A dated source states that the country has no national digital strategy, and none is on record as adopted, launched or in preparation.
A national digital strategy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor is in preparation.

A national digital strategy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A text the government has published, and no source calls a draft, counts as adopted. A strategy with no stated period stops here.

The strategy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against its own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the strategy's targets are published on every pillar within the past two years.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: HMIS

ladder.text: A dated source states that routine health reporting is not entered digitally at any level of the health system.

A digital reporting system is used by hospitals only or in some districts, or a national rollout is contracted or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use it, beyond pilot sites.
A national system takes the clinics' reports, which are keyed in at district level from the clinics' paper forms. A minority of primary clinics enter their own reports, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility, on a figure published within the past two years. Reporting completeness is published as well.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: EMR

ladder.text: A dated source states that patient records are kept on paper at every level of the health system.

Electronic patient records are in use in some hospitals or pilot facilities, or a national system is procured or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use them, beyond pilot sites.

Electronic patient records are in use in most hospitals, or in primary clinics in some districts, but each record stays in the facility that made it. A minority of primary clinics use them, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics keep electronic patient records, entered at the point of care. Each record is held under a unique patient identifier and can be retrieved at another facility.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics keep such shared records, on a figure published within the past two years. A record can be retrieved anywhere in the public network.
A dated source states that the country has no ICT or telecommunications sector policy, none is on record as adopted or in preparation, and no national digital strategy is held.
A sector policy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor sector policy is in preparation.
A sector policy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A policy with no stated period stops here. A national digital strategy is assessed on its own row and does not count.

The policy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against the policy's own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the policy's targets are published on every objective within the past two years.

digital.localgov--ict-infrastructure-for.label: ICT infrastructure for local government: office connection

ladder.text: A dated source states that local government offices have no connection of their own. Staff working on their own phones or modems does not change this.

A programme to connect local government offices is being prepared or piloted: equipment handed over, a contract signed or pilot offices connected. Or only the capital city or the regions above are connected.

Some local government offices outside the capital are connected, past any pilot, or work in a national system. They are a minority, or no share of local governments is published. A share equipped or covered by a programme, however high, places here.
More than half of local governments have a connection provided to the office by the state or the authority. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.

At least 90 per cent of local governments are connected and work in national systems over the connection, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural local governments.

digital.localgov--digitalisation-of-loca.label: Digitalisation of local government records: revenue records

ladder.text: A dated source states that local governments keep their revenue records on paper, with no system in use.
A system is being prepared or piloted, or a one-off survey has built a register with no system to keep it. Or only the capital city or the regions above record digitally.

Some local governments outside the capital record payments in a system, past any pilot. They are a minority, or no share is published. Electronic receipts with no register of payers place here, and so does a share given a system or trained on it, however high.
More than half of local governments keep a digital register of their payers, with each bill and payment against it. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local governments keep that register in a national or shared system, on a figure published within the past two years.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural police stations: station records

ladder.text: A dated source states that police stations record reports and cases on paper only. A fingerprint database, a crime statistics return or an online reporting portal does not change this.

A system for stations to record reports or cases is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot stations using it. Or one runs at headquarters or in the capital only.

Reports or cases are entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital; they are a minority, or no share of stations is published. A share of stations equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of stations enter reports or cases digitally at the station when they are taken, into the national system. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of stations do so, for both the first report and the case file, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural stations.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-r.label: Digitalisation of rural registry offices: civil registration

ladder.text: A dated source states that local civil registration offices register births and deaths on paper only. Scanning or keying old registers does not change this.
A system for local offices to register births digitally is being prepared or piloted, or one runs at the national office or in the capital only.

Births are entered digitally when they are registered, past any pilot, in some local offices; they are a minority, or no share of offices is published. A share of offices equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of local offices enter births digitally at the office when they are registered, into the national register. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local offices do so, for deaths as well as births, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural offices.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural primary schools: EMIS

ladder.text: A dated source states that primary schools keep their learners' records on paper only. An annual school census, however it is collected and whatever it is called, does not change this.
An EMIS for primary schools is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot schools using it. Or one runs in secondary schools only.

An EMIS is past its pilot and in live use in some primary schools, which enter attendance or results during the year; they are a minority, or no figure is published. Or schools past the pilot fill a national learner register once a year.
More than half of primary schools enter attendance or results for each learner during the school year, at the school. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of primary schools do so, with attendance entered daily, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural schools.

AGO.short: Law 7/17 of 2017 is in force and a new bill passed parliament in August 2026; no use of either is known.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. A UNITA deputy, quoted by Novo Jornal on 23 January 2026, says Law 7/17 of 16 February, on the protection of computer networks and systems, is part of the current legal order and that the new bill would repeal it. The Council of Ministers considered the Cybersecurity Bill on 27 October 2025 for sending to the National Assembly. The Assembly approved it in general terms on 23 January 2026, with 105 votes for and 75 UNITA abstentions, and adopted the cybersecurity law on 12 August 2026, with MPLA votes carrying it.

Use of the law. The law adopted on 12 August 2026 sets fines of 7 to 4,000 national minimum wages, by gravity, according to ANGOP. The National Assembly's specialised committees approved the proposed law before the final vote, as Telecompaper reported on 10 August 2026. PTI reports that the final vote of 12 August 2026 was taken globally, with 104 in favour.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BDI.short: A 2022 cybercrime law is in force and was cited as applied in 2026; no use against anyone is known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's cybercrime law is Law No. 1/10 of 16 March 2022 on the prevention and repression of cybercrime. At a workshop in Bujumbura in February 2026, a government delegate cited it as adopted and in application. A speaker at the same workshop said the president signed it in 2022. The law is named in the article as the country's cybercrime law, and the Malabo Convention was the standard against which the workshop measured it.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the same February 2026 workshop in Bujumbura, where experts and participants discussed the law's enforcement and its gaps against the Malabo Convention. The government delegate presented the law at that workshop as being in application. The article gives that discussion and the 2022 date of signature, and the law is the Burundian text on cybercrime prevention and repression adopted in March 2022.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BEN.short: The 2018 Code du numérique is in force; in 2025 about 1,500 online-fraud suspects were arrested.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, the Code du numérique, was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President. Its Livre VI defines illegal access to and penetration of an information system. The code carries the date 20 April 2018, and its Livre VI treats unauthorised entry into computer systems as an offence, in two forms: illegal access and penetration.

Use of the law. Benin's Centre national d'investigations numériques reported over 6,500 digital-offence complaints in 2025, against about 4,000 the year before, and about 1,500 arrests of online-fraud suspects. During INTERPOL's Operation Sentinel, from 27 October to 27 November 2025, Benin took down 43 malicious domains and shut 4,318 extortion and scam accounts, leading to 106 arrests. The complaints figure covers the whole of 2025, and the arrests figure covers suspects in online fraud.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

BFA.short: A 2024 information-security law is in force, with decrees adopted in July 2026; no use of it is known.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. The Council of Ministers of 30 July 2026 adopted decrees applying law n°014-2024/ALT of 9 July 2024 on the security of information systems. One identifies and categorises critical-infrastructure bodies, and the other sets periodic security audits and auditor accreditation. The law itself, headed Loi n°014-2024/ALT of 9 July 2024, sets rules to control and protect information systems and govern the actors in them, with licensing and fines.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the July 2026 decrees applying the law, which give it working machinery: a list of critical-infrastructure bodies to which the law applies, and periodic security audits carried out by accredited auditors. The licensing and fines that the law sets are the sanctions the law attaches to those actors. The Council of Ministers took the decisions on 30 July 2026, about two years after the law's date of 9 July 2024.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BWA.short: A cybersecurity law was enacted in November 2025 and replaces the 2018 cybercrime law; no use of it is known.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybersecurity Act, 2025 (Act No. 21 of 2025) was assented to on 5 November 2025 and gazetted on 11 November 2025. Its commencement is on a date the Minister appoints by Order, and it repeals and replaces the Cybercrime and Computer Related Crimes Act 2018. In March 2026 the communications minister said the Act was expected to come into force in April. Parliament had passed the Cybersecurity Bill, 2025 on 14 August 2025 under a certificate of urgency presented by the Minister of Communications and Innovation.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is that the ICT minister said, as ITWeb reported in May 2026, that the Act was passed in November 2025 and establishes a National Cybersecurity Authority. Botswana Daily News reported on 25 February 2026 that the Act, signed into law the year before, sets up that Authority.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CAF.short: A cybercrime law, Loi 24.002 of February 2024, is in force; a 2026 opinion piece says police and prosecutors use it. No case is known.
CAF.summary:
Law in force. The official laws index of the telecoms regulator ARCEP lists Loi 24.002 of 21 February 2024 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime among the country's laws. Africa Top Success reported that the National Assembly voted the cybersecurity and anti-cybercrime bill by acclamation on 25 January 2024, with promulgation by the President expected within days. The bill sets prison terms of 6 to 10 years and fines of 5 to 10 million CFA francs. In March 2023 terms of reference for a consultant described a draft law on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime that needed improving, and asked the consultant to draft amendments and implementing texts.

Use of the law. An opinion piece published on 18 August 2026 refers to the government's cybercrime law as wielded by the prosecutor's office and police. It dates from 2026, more than two years after the Assembly vote of January 2024.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CIV.short: A 2024 cybersecurity ordinance is in force; the cybercrime platform handled 12,100 files in 2024, with the law used not named.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Ordinance No. 2024-950, a cybersecurity text, is in force, and on 16 June 2025 the Senate unanimously adopted the bill ratifying it. The same bill updates the 2017 ordinance on electronic exchanges. The source describes the measure as a cybersecurity bill and reports no dissent in the vote.

Use of the law. The national information-security agency's report for 2024, presented on 22 May 2025, says its cybercrime platform received and handled 12,100 files in 2024, up from 8,132 the year before. The largest groups were 2,822 files on attacks on human dignity and 2,326 on online fraud, and the files also covered fraudulent access to information systems. The agency put the financial loss at about 7 billion CFA francs, down from more than 9 billion a year earlier. The report as relayed does not name the law the files were handled under.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided that names the law they were brought under, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

CMR.short: A cybercrime law from December 2010 is in force and was reviewed at a June 2026 workshop; no use against anyone is known.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. A Nkafu brief published on 4 September 2026 says Cameroon's legal framework is anchored in a 2010 cybersecurity law and 2012 decrees, and it calls for the 2010 law to be revised. The law is law no. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybercrime, which Le Jour treats as the existing law in Cameroon. The Nkafu brief of September 2026 and the Le Jour report of June 2026 therefore point to the same 2010 text as the law the country works under, a law dating from December 2010 that the brief wants revised, sixteen years before either piece appeared.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is a workshop reported by Le Jour on 16 June 2026. Held on 8 and 9 June 2026 in Yaounde, the workshop reviewed articles of law no. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybercrime.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COD.short: A digital code has been in force since 2023, and in August 2026 police were told to enforce it; no case is known.
COD.summary:
Law in force. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has the Code du numérique, promulgated in 2023. The news agency ACP states that the Code du numérique makes non-consensual sharing of intimate content, privacy breaches and cyberharassment criminal offences in the country. On 17 August 2026 the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation treated the Digital Code as in force, as the news agency ACP reported that same day.

Use of the law. On 17 August 2026 the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation told judicial police officers to take up offences under the Digital Code on their own initiative. This is an instruction to the officers who bring cases, issued in the Code's fourth year, and it covers the offences the Code creates. ACP also reports that the offences the Code du numérique names include cyberharassment and privacy breaches.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COG.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws of 2020 are in force; no arrest or case under them is known.
COG.summary:
Law in force. The Republic of the Congo has two laws of 5 June 2020, loi n° 26-2020 relative à la cybersécurité and loi n° 27-2020 portant lutte contre la cybercriminalité. The Journal officiel of 18 June 2026 prints a decree of 6 May 2026 that cites both as in force. The Journal officiel of 9 April 2026 prints decrees of 29 December 2025 that cite both the same way. The World Bank diagnostic of December 2020 says Loi 26-2020 governs the national legal framework for information-system and network security.

Use of the law. In its 2025 assessment, UNESCO states that application of the cybersecurity and cybercrime laws still has to be strengthened and calls for implementing texts for the cybercrime law. The same report cites no arrest, prosecution, conviction or case count under either law. The World Bank diagnostic adds that operationalising the bodies the cybersecurity law defines remained to be done in 2020.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COM.short: Cybercrime offences are in the Penal Code in force since 2021; a separate cybersecurity law was only a draft; no use is known.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The Comoros has cybercrime offences in its Penal Code. According to the national digital agency ANADEN, the President promulgated by decree on 16 February 2021 the new Penal Code, loi n°20-38/AU of 29 December 2020, whose articles 449 to 505 set out cybercrime offences, online intellectual property infringement and service-provider liability. The same ANADEN publication of 4 March 2021 lists a specific cybersecurity law as drafted but not yet adopted, to follow the Penal Code.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the promulgation itself. ANADEN states that the President promulgated the Penal Code by decree on 16 February 2021, with its cybercrime offences in articles 449 to 505. The same source gives the Penal Code as the first step, with a specific cybersecurity law and a digital code to follow. It records no case brought under these articles.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CPV.short: A 2021 cybersecurity decree-law is in force; no case under it is known.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. Cabo Verde has Decreto-lei n.º 9/2021, its regime jurídico de cibersegurança, together with Decreto-Regulamentar n.º 1/2021, which creates the national CSIRT. The 2026 State Budget law cites them as in place. The 2024 annual plan and budget of NOSi states that both decrees exist, and gives no further date for them. Both documents name the cybersecurity regime as a text that is already part of the country's rules.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is that the national CSIRT the regulating decree creates is named in official documents. The 2026 State Budget law cites Decreto-lei n.º 9/2021 and its regulating decree as in place, and the NOSi plan for 2024 lists them among existing texts. Neither document records any case brought under the law, and neither gives a date for any use of it by the authorities of Cabo Verde.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

DJI.short: A digital code with a cybercrime book passed parliament in 2025 but is only a bill so far; no use of it is known.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. Djibouti's National Assembly passed the Digital Code on 30 June 2025, covering cybersecurity and cybercrime and punishable online offences. The legislative section was still to be promulgated by the President and published in the Journal Officiel. TechAfrica News reported on 2 July 2025 that the Code has eight books and nearly 800 articles, and that Book VI deals with Cybersecurity and Cybercrime. It is Djibouti's first Digital Code and was passed in plenary.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is in the text itself: Jones Day reports, in a note of 1 July 2025, that the Digital Code makes online offences punishable. The Assembly adopted it on 30 June 2025, and the same report says its legislative section awaited promulgation by the President, then publication in the Journal Officiel. That adoption was reported within days: TechAfrica News carried it on 2 July 2025 under a headline saying Djibouti enacts the Code.

Not held. No source held says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force. Nothing is held on any arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under such a law.

DZA.short: A 2009 law on offences linked to information technology is treated as in force by a 2020 decree; no use of it is known.
DZA.summary:
Law in force. Algeria's Law 09-04 of 5 August 2009 sets out particular rules on preventing and fighting offences linked to information and communication technologies. Presidential decree 20-05 of 20 January 2020 lists it among the laws the decree rests on, and so treats it as standing law. The decree was published on 20 January 2020, the date it carries.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is the state's own reliance on the text, not a case brought under it. Presidential decree 20-05 of 20 January 2020 cites Law 09-04 of 5 August 2009 among the laws it rests on, which shows the executive treating the law as current in 2020. The law's French title is the Loi n° 09-04 du 5 août 2009 portant règles particulières relatives à la prévention et à la lutte contre les infractions liées aux technologies de l'information et de la communication.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

EGY.short: A 2018 law on information technology crimes is in force; two bills in April 2026 would amend it. No use of it is known.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt's Law 175 of 2018 on combating information technology crimes is treated as the current law in a bill an MP put forward on 22 April 2026, which would tighten its provisions. A separate bill from an MP, referred to committees by the House speaker, also amends Law 175, which its sponsor calls the current law, with penalties too weak.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is amendment, not enforcement. Both bills take Law 175 of 2018 as the baseline to be changed, one to tighten its provisions and one, according to its sponsor, because the penalties are too weak. Both were reported on the same day, 22 April 2026, by Egyptian outlets El Watan News and El Balad. The House speaker referred the second bill to committees in April 2026, and the law remains the current text while it is amended.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

ERI.short: No cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill is known for Eritrea, and no use of one is known.
ERI.summary: Not held. No law or bill is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has neither. Any use of such a law is also not held.

ETH.short: A critical infrastructure cybersecurity law was passed in July 2026 and takes effect in July 2027; no use of it is known.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. The Federal Negarit Gazette, 32nd Year No. 41 carries Critical Infrastructure Cyber Security Protection Proclamation No. 1426/2026, done at Addis Ababa on 21 July 2026 and signed by the President. Its article 28 provides that it enters into force one year after publication, which puts commencement in July 2027. INSA's Director General said on 7 August 2026 that the House of People's Representatives unanimously ratified the proclamation, which sets 18 obligations for owners of 12 critical sectors.

Use of the law. The nearest fact held is that, according to INSA's Director General, institutions are to use a transition period to prepare for compliance with the proclamation's 18 obligations. The gazette text places entry into force one year after publication, so the transition runs until July 2027. The proclamation is a critical infrastructure measure for 12 sectors, under which owners face 18 obligations.

Not held. No source held says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

GAB.short: A cybersecurity and cybercrime law, numbered 027/2023, was in force in 2025; no use of it against anyone is known.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabonreview, in an article published on 1 June 2025, presents law no. 027/2023 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime as a national law. It is the law with which ANINF's SecBOM, the Security Bill of Material, must comply. The article treats the law as the standing national framework for cybersecurity in Gabon, and names ANINF as the agency whose tool is held to it. ANINF is described there as reinforcing national cybersecurity through the SecBOM, a tool on which the article reports.

Use of the law. The nearest fact held is the same article of 1 June 2025, which links the law to ANINF's SecBOM: the tool must comply with law no. 027/2023. That is a compliance requirement placed on an agency tool, stated in a news article, and it is the only application of the law described in the source.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

GHA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2026 the authority fined a state registry and a private firm under it.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Digital Policy Alert states that Ghana's 2020 Cybersecurity Act establishes measures for critical information infrastructure protection, cybercrime prevention and incident response, and that Ghana implemented the Act. It names the Cyber Security Authority as the body created under the Act. In August 2026 the Cyber Security Authority sanctioned bodies under Section 92 of the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), which the article treats as the law in force.

Use of the law. In an article published on 13 August 2026, the Cyber Security Authority fined the Office of the Registrar of Companies GH¢240,000, being 10,000 penalty units for each of two instances of non-compliance under Section 92(2) of Act 1038. It also fined Purpleline Solutions Limited GH¢120,000 for providing cybersecurity services without a licence. Both were fined as bodies, one a state office and one a private company.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

GIN.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2025 the media regulator said it will be used against web media.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. The president of the Haute Autorité de la Communication said in July 2025 that the cybersecurity law, and not the press law, will be applied to web media that break the rules. The same statement, reported by Aminata on 26 July 2025, says the penalty is prison for any person. The law is referred to as the loi sur la cybersécurité, and the statement treats it as the one that governs web media conduct today.

Use of the law. The nearest fact held is the same statement of July 2025, in which the president of the Haute Autorité de la Communication said the law will be applied to web media that break the rules, with prison for any person. It is a statement of how the law is to be applied to online media, made by the media regulator's head.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

GMB.short: A 2009 act with cybercrime offences is in force and a 2024 cybercrime bill is not enacted; no use of either is known.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Information and Communications Act, 2009 (No. 2 of 2009) entered into force on 29 May 2009. Its Part III of Chapter III, "Computer Misuse and Cyber Crime", creates offences such as unauthorised access to computer data. Parliament introduced a proposed Cybercrime Bill in March 2024, and the Oxford Institute of Technology and Justice states that, as at June 2026, it has not been enacted. That Bill is the latest development held on a dedicated cybercrime statute, and it is dated June 2026.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the penalty the Act's offences carry: unauthorised access to computer data is punishable by a fine of 200,000 dalasis or up to five years' imprisonment, or both. Separately, The Gambia signed the African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection on 2 December 2022, a continental treaty covering both subjects.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

GNB.short: A cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill is not known, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not held. Nothing names a cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill for Guinea-Bissau, or says there is none.

GNQ.short: Ley 7/2024 is in force; in September 2026 the vice-president's lawyers filed four complaints under it, including against Diario Rombe.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. The Government stated on 1 July 2026 that Ley 7/2024 of 23 December 2024, regulating social networks, computer crimes and cybercrime, is fully in force. In September 2026 a law firm treated it as applicable law, grounding complaints on its articles 2, 50 and 60.

Use of the law. On 16 September 2026, lawyers acting for vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue lodged four criminal complaints under Ley 7/2024 at Juzgado de Instruccion Numero I de Malabo. They name Maria Luzmila Ondo, Mocache Massoko of Diario Rombe, Jose Carlos Ndong and Maria Teresa Siemfum. The case is at an initial stage, awaiting the court. The complainant is the vice-president himself, so the use held is a case brought by a senior state official against four named people, one of them from the Diario Rombe outlet. The law's own title covers social networks, computer crimes and cybercrime together.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years.

KEN.short: The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act is in force; a September 2026 guide covers prosecuting 76 offences. No prosecution under it is known.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act stands. On 3 September 2026 Kenya launched an official guide to investigating and prosecuting 76 listed cyber offences under it, presented as the common operational framework under the Act. The Nation reports that it has been amended, widening investigators' and courts' powers. Two false-publication sections were struck down by the Court of Appeal, and the Act otherwise stands.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the machinery built on the Act: Kenya's cybersecurity framework rests on the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee under the Act, to which the new National Cybersecurity Agency (Legal Notice 89 of 2026) adds capacity. The Act was also put in place to address risks on digital platforms. Both items date from September 2026, the same month as the prosecution guide, and the Committee and the Agency sit side by side in that framework.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

LBR.short: Cybercrime law in force since 2026; used in September 2026 to arrest a commentator over images of the Vice President.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's Cybercrime Act of 2025 was signed into law by President Boakai in 2026, and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications has published the approved Act. One report says the Act requires regulations within six to twelve months, and another says the country has entered the enforcement phase. The Act is being operationalized by the Liberia Telecommunications Authority and the Ministry of Justice, and ten civil society organisations plan to engage lawmakers on amendments.

Use of the law. In September 2026 police arrested the commentator Jerry Nyantee Wrato over AI-generated images of the Vice President, then charging him and forwarding him to court. The Inspector General's letter of 21 September resolved to prosecute him under sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Act, covering misuse of devices, cyberstalking, incitement and harmful data messages. A court ordered him released on habeas corpus on 22 September. The arrest was presented as the Act's first major public test.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

LBY.short: A parliamentary committee was preparing a cybersecurity bill in July 2026; no law in force is known, and no use of one.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya's nearest held fact is a bill. On 15 July 2026 a temporary House of Representatives committee met National Security Council officials in Benghazi to work on preparing a comprehensive cybersecurity bill. The committee was created by Speaker's decision 115 of 2025. The report describes a bill in preparation, not an enacted law, and the work it records sits at the stage of drafting, with the National Security Council officials taking part in the meeting held in Benghazi in the middle of July 2026.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact concerns the bill rather than a law in operation. The House of Representatives committee, created by Speaker's decision 115 of 2025, met National Security Council officials in Benghazi on 15 July 2026 to prepare a comprehensive cybersecurity bill. The document reports a bill in preparation, not an enacted law.

Not held. No source held says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

LSO.short: Cybercrime and cybersecurity bills were still awaiting Parliament in September 2026; no law in force is known, and no use of one.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. Lesotho's nearest held fact is a pair of bills. Cabinet split the 2024 bill into a Cybercrime Bill 2026 and a Cybersecurity Bill 2026, and the Department of Information reports a second stakeholder consultation on the Cybersecurity Bill 2026 after a draft circulated in August 2026, with the bill still to proceed through the next legislative stages. The Lesotho Times reports that a 2021 version was withdrawn from Parliament and the 2024 Computer Crime and Cyber Security Bill was referred to Parliament but not enacted. In August 2026 the Director General of ICT said both bills were ready and waiting for approval by the National Assembly.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact concerns the draft text. The Computer Crime and Cyber Security Bill, 2024 would commence on gazettal and be cited as the Act once enacted. In January 2026 the Principal Secretary at the communications ministry said it was working on the Cybersecurity Bill.

Not held. No source held says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

MAR.short: Morocco's cybersecurity law of 2020 is in force, with an implementing decree in force by February 2025; no use of it is known.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. Morocco's Loi n° 05-20 on cybersecurity was promulgated by dahir n° 1-20-69 of 25 July 2020 and published in Bulletin officiel n° 6906 of 6 August 2020. Its article 53 makes it operative on publication of its implementing texts. The same page records that décret n° 2-24-921, applying article 25, was in force by the Bulletin officiel of 20 February 2025, so the law has implementing texts in place alongside the 2020 text.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the law's own implementation. Loi n° 05-20 becomes operative on publication of its implementing texts under article 53, and décret n° 2-24-921, which applies article 25, was in force by the Bulletin officiel of 20 February 2025. The page lists the law under the Kingdom of Morocco, with the dahir of 25 July 2020 as its promulgation and Bulletin officiel n° 6906 of 6 August 2020 as its publication, and the 2025 decree as the later implementing text it records.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MDG.short: A 2014 cybercrime law is in force; a replacement bill was postponed in September 2026. No use of the law is known.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Madagascar's cybercrime framework still rests in part on loi n°2014-006, adopted in June 2014, which defined offences such as fraudulent access to information systems and data breaches. The government tabled bill n°042/2026 on combating cybercrime at the National Assembly on 28 August 2026, with penalties of two to ten years and fines of 100,000 to 100 million ariary. The Council of Ministers had adopted the draft bill recasting the law on 7 July 2026. On 4 September deputies voted to postpone adoption of the 96-article text, and it was not among the 17 bills on the agenda of the extraordinary session opening 17 September 2026.

Use of the law. The 2026 bill would create the Upin digital police. A digital-law specialist interviewed by Midi Madagasikara says it would require suspicious-transaction reports on Mobile Money transfers of 10 million ariary or more and tighten SIM identification.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MLI.short: Cybercrime provisions sit in the penal code since December 2024; in 2026 they were used against journalists, including a 12-month sentence in August.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. IPI states that Mali amended its Penal Code in December 2024, incorporating provisions previously contained in the 2019 cybercrime law, and that journalists have been arrested and imprisoned under the new penal code.

Use of the law. Journalist Chahana Takiou, founder-director of the newspaper 22 septembre, was sentenced on 3 August 2026 to 12 months in prison, 6 suspended, for undermining the credit of the State, after the cybercrime pole summoned him. IPI reports that journalist Abdrahamane Keita of Le Témoin was detained on 9 June 2026 and charged with undermining national unity and the credibility of the state and spreading false information, with his trial postponed from 17 to 31 August, and that the trial of commentator Mohamed Youssouf Bathily began on 10 August 2026. The criminal chamber of the cybercrime pole had 4 cases involving 8 accused on its roll on 21 May 2026.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

MOZ.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws were signed in 2026. No use of the law is known.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. President Chapo promulgated the Cybersecurity Law in June 2026, protecting networks, information systems and critical infrastructure, with a regulatory body and penalties up to 160 minimum wages. Africa AI News states that Mozambique already has a Cyber Security Act and a Cybercrimes Act as part of its legal foundation. The Penal Code (Law 24/2019, amended by Law 17/2020) also provides cybercrimes such as database intrusion, punishable by up to two years, and electronic fraud, punishable by one to five years.

Use of the law. On 28 July 2026 the communications minister said the government has approved the Cybersecurity Law and the Cybercrime Law and that implementation is mandatory for companies operating critical infrastructure. In April 2026 Parliament unanimously approved the Cyber Security Law, making INCM technical coordinator for cyberspace security and creating a Cyber Security Fund, a proposal the government had submitted the previous Thursday.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MRT.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2016. No use of the law is known.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2016-007 on cybercrime was adopted by the National Assembly and the Senate and promulgated by the President of the Republic. It has 52 articles covering offences, search and interception powers, and international cooperation. The year, 2016, is taken from the law number, and the law is cited as Loi n° 2016-007 relative à la cybercriminalité. Its provisions on offences sit beside its provisions on how investigators may search and intercept, and its provisions on how the state cooperates with other countries.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the content of the same 2016 cybercrime law: its 52 articles give search and interception powers, alongside the offences it defines and its provisions on international cooperation. Both chambers of the legislature adopted it before the President promulgated it, so the text that gives investigators those powers is a promulgated law and not a draft.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MUS.short: A cybercrime and cybersecurity law has been in force since December 2021; no case under it is known.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. The Cybersecurity and Cybercrime Act 2021 (Act No. 16 of 2021) was passed by the National Assembly on 19 November 2021, assented to on 24 November 2021 and gazetted as Legal Supplement 567; the retrieved text records it as proclaimed in force on 10 December 2021, and it repeals the Computer Misuse and Cybercrime Act. On 7 October 2026 the Ministry of Technology, Communication and Innovation discussed proposed amendments to the Act with Meta in Ebene.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is how the Act is relied on. The Ministry treats the Act as the operating legal framework for online content, the subject of its October 2026 working session with Meta. The National Crime Agency Bill text published by the National Assembly in September 2026 defines cybercrime by reference to offences under Part III of the Act, the same offences the Act sets out.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MWI.short: A cybercrime and cybersecurity law has been in force since 2017; no case under it is known.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. Malawi's Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act, Act 33 of 2016 and Chapter 74:02 of the laws, is the country's statute on computer and ICT offences. The Act was published in the Gazette on 4 November 2016 and commenced on 1 June 2017. It criminalises offences related to computer systems and ICT, and it does so within a single statute that also covers electronic transactions, as its title shows.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is the Act's commencement. The Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act took effect on 1 June 2017, more than nine years before October 2026, and it remains the Act that criminalises offences related to computer systems and ICT. Its text is published by the Malawi Legal Information Institute, which gives the Gazette date of 4 November 2016 and the Act number, 33 of 2016.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

NAM.short: Only a cybercrime bill is known, under consultation in 2026; no law in force is known, so no use of one.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. No cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force is known. The proposed law is the Namibia Cybercrime Bill. NAM-CSIRT's 2025 landscape report says that in the absence of a cybersecurity law in Namibia it looks to the government to expedite the Cybercrime Bill and related regulations, and it recommends finalising and enacting the Cybercrime, Data Protection and CII regulations. NAMPA reports that the Namibia Cybercrime Bill is not yet law.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is the consultation on the bill. In February 2026 the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology consulted stakeholders from Kavango East, Kavango West and Zambezi at Rundu on the proposed cybersecurity and cybercrime bill. Namibia's computer incident response team, NAM-CSIRT, published its 2025 cybersecurity landscape report and, dated by its publication in April 2026, it asks the government to expedite the Cybercrime Bill alongside related regulations.

Not held. No source held says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

NER.short: A 2019 cybercrime law is in force; in October 2025 it was used to charge six journalists.
NER.summary:
Law in force. Niger has a cybercrime law dating from 2019. The military authorities amended it in 2024 to restore prison terms of up to five years and fines for disseminating data likely to disturb public order, and Human Rights Watch reports it was the law under which charges were brought in October 2025. The law is in force and the authorities apply it, including its public-order offence of disseminating data, with the charges dated to 30 October 2025.

Use of the law. The law was used against journalists. Per Human Rights Watch, police in Niamey arrested six journalists on 30 October 2025 and the authorities charged them with complicity in disseminating a document likely to disturb public order under the 2019 cybercrime law, for sharing an invitation to a state press conference. Three of the six were detained at Kollo prison, and the arrests took place in Niamey, the capital, on a single day.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

NGA.short: A cybercrime law is in force and was used in 2026 against activist Omoyele Sowore, and in 2024 against journalists and critics.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act is an enacted law of 2015 and was amended in 2024. The amended Act contains interception provisions, and SERAP says the 2024 amendment retains ambiguous cyberstalking wording in section 24. Section 24 prescribes up to three years' imprisonment or a fine for sending a message known to be false.

Use of the law. The Act has been used against critics, journalists and activists. In December 2024 activist Olamide Thomas was arrested and charged for allegedly insulting the President's son on Facebook. The Department of State Services is prosecuting activist and presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore over his description of the President as a criminal, and its Director-General announced on 30 August 2026 that the prosecution would be suspended until after the 2027 election. SERAP says authorities continue to use section 24 to arrest and charge journalists, bloggers, activists and ordinary citizens. Reporters Without Borders reported in 2024 that at least eight journalists had been arrested, prosecuted or detained under the Act.

Not held. The number of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law in a period ending in the last two years.

RWA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force, as of 2026. Whether it has been used is not known.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda has a cybersecurity law in force. The East African Policy Observer, drawing on the Carnegie Endowment's Africa Technology Policy Tracker, says Rwanda's binding legal instruments include cybersecurity law. The commentary was published on 30 July 2026 and reviews Rwanda, Nigeria and Zambia together. It adds that all three countries reviewed have cybersecurity laws.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the same statement of July 2026: Rwanda's binding legal instruments include cybersecurity law, and Rwanda is one of the three countries the commentary says have cybersecurity laws. Published on 30 July 2026 by the East African Policy Observer, the commentary reports on Rwanda, Nigeria and Zambia and draws on the Carnegie Endowment's Africa Technology Policy Tracker and describes the law as one of Rwanda's binding legal instruments, listed beside the two other countries it reviews.

Not held. Any arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

SDN.short: A cybercrime law is in force and was used in 2026 to jail a pharmacist over anti-war messages and to arrest a journalist.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. Sudan has a Cybercrime Law, and courts apply it: a criminal court in El Obeid convicted a defendant under Articles 19 and 24 in August 2026. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate cites the Cybercrime Act as the basis of a live arrest and calls for its repeal. The SudaPass terms cite the Cybercrime Law as the basis of criminal penalties of up to twelve years for electronic sabotage or forgery, and refer to a Cyber Security Act of 2025.

Use of the law. The law has been used against an anti-war critic and a journalist. In August 2026 a criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed Al-Waqi to six years in total, two of them under Article 19 and one under Article 24 of the Cybercrime Law, after a phone search found anti-war messages, according to his lawyer. In August 2026 criminal investigation police arrested journalist Gurashi Awad in River Nile State on a complaint by a General Intelligence Service lieutenant colonel, the Sudanese Journalists Syndicate said.

Not held. The number of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law in a period ending in the last two years.

SEN.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2008 and a cybersecurity bill is before the Assembly in 2026. Its use is not known.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. Senegal's Cybercrime Law, Law 2008-10 of 25 January 2008, completes the Penal Code and the Penal Procedure Code and lists offences with penalties of six months to 10 years. The same 2018 practitioner source says no separate cybersecurity act had yet been adopted. In August 2026 the Ministry of Telecommunications and Digital Economy submitted a bill on the protection of critical information infrastructure and digital security to the National Assembly's Intercommission, which would set up a National Cybersecurity Authority and CERTs.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the list of what the law covers: the Cybercrime Law of 2008 lists the offences it creates and sets penalties from six months to 10 years. It was adopted to complete the Penal Code and the Penal Procedure Code, so its offences sit beside the general criminal law.

Not held. Any arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

SLE.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2021; no case under it is known.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone has a cybercrime law in force. The Cyber Security and Crime Act, 2021 was published as a supplement to the Gazette dated 25 November 2021, setting up a response coordination centre, an advisory council and a fund, and defining offences. The national development plan lists the Cybercrime Act 2021 among its sector milestones, and the digital development strategy says the bill drafted in 2018 was signed into law in 2021.

Use of the law. The national data strategy, published in January 2023, calls for capacity to implement the Cybersecurity and Cybercrimes Act, 2021. The digital development strategy lists operationalising the institutions the law sets up: the Council, NC3, NCSIRCC and the Fund. A World Bank project document of October 2021 lists the Cybercrime Law (2021) as progress, with a Cybersecurity Emergency Response Center still to be set up.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SOM.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime bills have moved through parliament since 2025; no law in force is known, and no use is known.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia has bills before parliament. The National Communications Authority states the House of the People approved the Cybersecurity Law on 26 January 2026. On 29 August 2026 the Senate held first reading of a six-chapter, 33-article cybersecurity bill, which still needs second and third readings before final approval. The House of the People concluded first reading of the Cybercrimes Bill on 8 December 2025 and sent it to committee.

Use of the law. The nearest held facts concern the bills. A news report says the House approved the Cybersecurity Law on 26 January 2026 and that the government approved a draft cybercrime bill in August 2025. A second report says parliament approved the Cybersecurity Law in January 2026 and that a cybercrime bill passed in August 2025. A third report, on the launch of the national incident response team, also says parliament approved the Cybersecurity Law in January 2026 and that a cybercrime bill was approved in August 2025.

Not held. No source says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force. No use of any such law is known.

SSD.short: A cybercrime law was signed in February 2026 and put into operation in July 2026; no case under it is known.
SSD.summary:
Law in force. South Sudan has a cybercrime law in force. Radio Tamazuj reports that President Kiir signed the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 on 18 February 2026 and that it came into force on signature. Its offences and penalties sit in Chapter Six, and Chapter 5 sets critical infrastructure designation, 24-hour incident reporting and administrative penalties. The Information Minister said the law is in effect. Parliament had passed the bill on 25 November 2025.

Use of the law. Eye Radio reports that the government announced implementation of the Act in July 2026, amid free expression concerns. Under Presidential Directive No. 03 of 2026 the National Cyber-Security Task Force held its first operational meeting on 16 July 2026. In September 2026 more than 20 civil society, security and media participants were trained in Yei River County on the Act, which the report treats as current law.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

STP.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2017; no case under it is known.
STP.summary:
Law in force. Sao Tome and Principe has a cybercrime law in force. Lei n.º 15/2017, the Lei sobre Cibercrime, was passed by the Assembleia Nacional on 28 June 2017, promulgated on 3 August 2017 and published in the Diário da República on 6 October 2017. It creates computer-crime offences and procedural powers, and it enters into force 30 days after publication, about 5 November 2017.

Use of the law. The same law is the nearest held fact on use. It gives the Polícia Judiciária a round-the-clock contact point, available twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, for the procedural powers it creates, and the Assembleia Nacional passed the law itself. The law was passed in June 2017 and published in October 2017, and it creates computer-crime offences and procedural powers that apply from about November 2017, when it enters into force.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SWZ.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since March 2022; officials say arrests are possible, but no case under it is known.
SWZ.summary:
Law in force. The Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act, 2022 (Act No. 6 of 2022) was published in the Government Gazette Extraordinary on 4 March 2022 and, by section 1(2), came into operation on the date of publication. On 1 October 2026 the Director of Public Prosecutions described the Act as the legal framework for offences committed through or against computer systems. The Act has therefore stood as Eswatini's cybercrime law since March 2022, and officials still cite it as the governing text in 2026.

Use of the law. On 27 August 2026 an officer of the communications regulator ESCCOM said that cyberbullying is a crime under the Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act of 2022 and that people can be arrested for it. The Director of Public Prosecutions said on 1 October 2026 that her office has trained prosecutors on the Act. These are official statements on how the law applies and on preparing prosecutors to use it.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SYC.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2022 and was widened in December 2025; no case under it is known.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes and Other Related Crimes Act 2021 (Act 59 of 2021) was assented on 15 December 2021 and repeals the Computer Misuse Act (Cap 254). Act 23 of 2025 amends it. The National Assembly passed that amendment on 15 December 2025 and the President assented to it on 22 December 2025. It widens the offences and amends an Act already in operation, so Seychelles has a working cybercrime statute that was extended at the end of 2025.

Use of the law. The 2025 amendment, assented on 22 December 2025, adds search and interception powers to the Act alongside the wider offences. These are powers for investigating offences under it. The amendment states no commencement date of its own. Both texts are published in the official gazette. They sit on top of the 2021 Act, which replaced the earlier Computer Misuse Act, Cap 254.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TCD.short: A cybercrime law from 2015 is listed among Chad's laws; whether it has been used is not known.
TCD.summary:
Law in force. The sector regulator ARCEP's register of laws lists Loi N°009/PR/2015 on Cybersecurity and the Fight against Cybercrime among Chad's laws. The register names the law as Loi N°009/PR/2015 portant sur la Cybersécurité et la Lutte Contre la Cybercriminalité. The year 2015 is the year in the law's number. Chad's regulator therefore carries a national cybersecurity and cybercrime law on its list of the laws that apply in the country.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on how the law is applied is its place in the same ARCEP register of laws, where the regulator lists it among Chad's laws alongside the rest of the legal framework for the sector. The law is presented there as part of the framework the regulator works within, in the 2015 numbering, under the title covering both cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TGO.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2018, amended in 2022; no case under it is known.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2018-026 of 7 December 2018 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime was promulgated and published in the Journal officiel, setting the cybersecurity framework and defining and punishing cybercrime offences. Loi n° 2022-009 of 24 June 2022, adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President, amends articles 2, 3 and 6 of it. The 2018 text was issued as a special number of the Journal officiel and remains the base text that the 2022 law modifies.

Use of the law. The visas of Décret n° 2022-094/PR of 9 September 2022 cite the 2018 law as modified by the 2022 law, treating it as standing law. The government thus relies on it in later regulation, which is a use of the text as a legal basis. The decree cites both the 2018 law and the 2022 amendment as current, within three months of the amendment.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TUN.short: A cybersecurity decree-law has been in force in Tunisia since 2023; no case under it is known.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Decree-law no. 2023-17 of 11 March 2023 on cybersecurity, published in JORT no. 26, is in force: its Article 30 brings it into force six months after publication, and the database record gives its status as in force. It sets audit, labelling, classification, incident-response and critical-infrastructure duties for public and private bodies. The database lists it under its French title, Décret-loi n° 2023-17 du 11 mars 2023, relatif à la cybersécurité.

Use of the law. The decree-law puts its duties on the public and private bodies listed in Article 6 and sets fines of 50,000 to 100,000 dinars. The Agence nationale de la cybersécurité (ANCS), supervised by the Ministry of Communication Technologies, replaces the Agence nationale de la sécurité informatique under this text. The earlier agency is a state body, and the list of covered bodies sits in Article 6 of the decree-law.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TZA.short: A cybercrime law has been in force in Tanzania since 2015; no case under it is known.
TZA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes Act (Cap. 443, Revised Edition 2023, originally Act No. 14 of 2015) states that it commenced on 1 September 2015 under GN No. 528 of 2015. It applies to Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, and it criminalises illegal access, interception, data interference, fraud and forgery. The consolidated text is the Revised Edition 2023 held by the Office of the Attorney General, and the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology cites the Act in 2026.

Use of the law. The ICT Minister said on 19 August 2026 that section 29 of the Cybercrimes Act provides a fine of not less than 100m/- or three times the damage, imprisonment of at least five years, or both, for damaging critical ICT infrastructure. The Ministry of Information and Communication Technology owns the Act in that report. The minister's statement concerns owners and operators of critical ICT infrastructure, for whom the Ministry has set up a registration system.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

UGA.short: The Computer Misuse Act is in force, and in 2026 police arrested three men over alleged fake news and personal data posts.
UGA.summary:
Law in force. Uganda's Constitutional Court struck down Sections 11, 23, 26, 27, 28 and 29 of the Computer Misuse Act and Sections 162 and 163 of the Penal Code Act (criminal libel), leaving the rest of the Act standing. Nilepost says the cyber-offence framework is anchored in the Computer Misuse Act, 2011 as amended in 2022, with some offences carrying up to 10 years in prison. The Nilepost account is dated 1 September 2026. A July 2026 joint UPR submission urges repeal or amendment of sections 24 and 25.

Use of the law. In September 2026 Kampala Metropolitan Police arrested and held three men over alleged fake news and unlawful obtaining or disclosure of personal data on social media, in an investigation the report places under the Computer Misuse Act. The incidents date to July 2026, and charges were not disclosed.

Not held. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

ZAF.short: A cybercrime law was reported in force in 2026; no case under it is known.
ZAF.summary:
Law in force. IOL, in an article dated 16 September 2026 on whether South Africa will ban under-16s from social media, reports the Cybercrimes Act (2020) as an existing South African law. The report describes the Act as already providing protections, and it gives no other date for that statement.

Use of the law. The same IOL report says the Cybercrimes Act (2020) deals with hacking, online fraud and sharing intimate images without consent. It presents these as protections that South Africa already has, and it makes the point in answer to the question of a social media ban for under-16s. The article is dated 16 September 2026, and IOL presents the Act as law already in place on that date, under the name Cybercrimes Act and the year 2020, as its own statement and not a quotation of the text.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

ZMB.short: Two cyber laws passed in 2025 are in force; no arrest or charge under them is known.
ZMB.summary:
Law in force. Zambia has a Cyber Crimes Act and a Cyber Security Act, both of 2025, which replaced the 2021 Cyber Security and Cybercrime Act. On 5 August 2026 Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition noted the enactment of the Cybercrimes Act and the Cybersecurity Act. In July 2026 the opposition running mate Makebi Zulu said that, if elected, his government would repeal the Cyber Crimes and Cyber Security Act.

Use of the law. Critics have warned about how the Acts may be used. Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition urged the government on 5 August 2026 not to let the two Acts become tools to suppress expression. At a rally before 4 July 2026, Makebi Zulu said the Act had gagged Zambians since its enactment, and that his government would repeal it if elected, a pledge reported by the Diggers news site in July 2026.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is known.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe has no separate cybercrime act; cybercrime offences in the criminal code, amended 2021, are in force; no case of use is known.
ZWE.summary:
Law in force. On 24 January 2026 the Director General of POTRAZ stated that Zimbabwe has no standalone cyber crimes act. Cybercrime offences are in force instead in Part VIII of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], as amended in 2021. They cover hacking, data interference, cyber-bullying, child abuse material and others, in sections 163 to 168.

Use of the law. The cybercrime provisions in force are the offences in Part VIII of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, sections 163 to 168. The POTRAZ Director General set them out on 24 January 2026 while stating that the country has no separate cyber crimes act. They include hacking, data interference, cyber-bullying and child abuse material. The Act, as amended in 2021, is the law in force on these offences, according to the Director General, who gave the date of 24 January 2026 for his statement.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is known.

AGO.short: Angola has an authority, appointed in 2019, that fined companies in 2025 and 2026; no yearly count of its rulings is known at September 2026.
AGO.summary:
Named in law and appointed. Lei 22/11 of 17 June 2011 created the Agência de Protecção de Dados as a public-law body with a seven-member board. Decreto Presidencial 214/16 set out its statute, and Decreto Presidencial 277/19 of 6 September 2019 appointed a president and two executive administrators. In 2024 its president signed Circular 02/APD/2024 requiring entities to report personal data breaches, and its FAQ page directs citizens to lodge complaints with it.

Rulings and published figures. The authority fined Lizíria, Lda., owner of Hotel Diamante, the kwanza equivalent of USD 115,000 on 10 August 2026. In June 2026 it fined Crescer Tech about USD 505,000 and Fast Digital Center USD 112,000. Its own register lists 15 fines for 2022 to 2026, six of them in 2026, from US$75,000 to US$525,000 each.

Not held. No count of the authority's decisions, fines or complaints settled, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2026 law creates an authority, but no appointment, ruling or published figure is known.
BDI.summary:
Named in law and appointed. The law adopted on 15 January 2026 creates an independent administrative authority responsible for enforcing data protection. It also provides a dedicated body to implement and monitor data protection regimes, and the sponsoring ministry was the Ministry of Interior, Community Development and Public Security. The law was promulgated on 10 March 2026. The sources held name no head or member of the authority and report no appointment, so the authority is set out in law only.

Rulings and published figures. No ruling against an organisation and no published figure is held. The nearest fact is that the adopted law makes the authority responsible for enforcement, and the law took effect by promulgation in March 2026.

Not held. No source held says the authority's head or members have been appointed.

BEN.short: Benin has an authority with a sitting president in 2026, and it published figures for its work in 2025.
BEN.summary:
Named in law and appointed. Book V of the Digital Code, Articles 462 to 473, established the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles as an independent administrative authority. It has a sitting head: president Luciano Hounkponou led a delegation to Lomé on 2 and 3 October 2026. Seventeen of its officers were sworn in on 14 September 2026. The 2026 finance law opens a programme for it at XOF 738,277,000.

Rulings and published figures. The authority's published 2025 report gives 907 files examined, 64 inspection missions, 20 complaints treated and 75 compliance certificates issued. Its 2015 to 2020 report counts 347 decisions, 136 of them in 2020. On 18 August 2016 it refused Spacetel Benin authorisation to collect biometric subscriber data.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso has an authority, active in 2025; no ruling against an organisation is known, and no figures it publishes are known.
BFA.summary:
Named in law and appointed. Law no. 001-2021/AN creates the Commission de l'informatique et des libertés (CIL) as the supervisory authority, with nine members appointed by decree. It is at work: its president led a training for a minister's cabinet on 11 August 2025, and the 2024 finance law gives it its own budget section. On 3 August 2026 the legislative assembly adopted a bill merging the CIL into a new regulator, ARCOD.

Rulings and published figures. A guide to the 2021 law says the CIL may issue warnings, formal notices, injunctions and fines. No ruling against a named organisation is held. The figures held are budget figures: the 2024 finance law appropriated XOF 857,062,000 for the CIL and 799,459,500 was executed, and the mid-year review at 30 June 2025 lists it again.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held. Whether ARCOD's members have been appointed is not known, and the CIL is counted until a source says it has gone.

BWA.short: Botswana has an authority, and in July 2026 it ruled against a government body; no figures it publishes are known.
BWA.summary:
Named in law and appointed. The Information and Data Protection Commission works under the Data Protection Act No. 18 of 2024. The Minister said it was established in 2022, and in July 2025 its commissioner had three contract officers while the deputy commissioner and two director posts were unfilled. Mmegi reported on 11 February 2026 that Kepaletswe Somolekae is the newly appointed commissioner. In July 2026 it reviewed the E-Payslip portal and guided DPSM through compliance.

Rulings and published figures. In a public notice dated 17 July 2026 the commission issued a Determination and an Enforcement Notice against DPSM for contraventions of the Act. It ordered the ePayslip portal suspended and a data protection impact assessment and revised privacy notice submitted within one month, with an administrative fine possible for non-compliance. DPSM suspended the portal on 22 July 2026. No published figures are held.

Not held. No count of the authority's decisions, fines or complaints settled, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic had no authority appointed in January 2026; no ruling against an organisation and no published figures are known.
CAF.summary:
Named in law and appointed. Article 57 of Loi n° 24.001 gives the ministry in charge of the digital economy twelve months from promulgation to set up the data protection agency, and meanwhile vests the agency's missions in that ministry. The text names no composition, seat or financing. Data Protection Africa states that the authority has not yet been appointed, as of 28 January 2026.

Rulings and published figures. The nearest held fact is that, under the same article, the ministry holds the agency's missions in the meantime. The law was promulgated in January 2024. No ruling against an organisation and no published figures are held, and no agency has yet issued any decision or report that a source records.

Not held. No source held says the authority's head or members have been appointed.

CIV.short: In 2026 Côte d'Ivoire's telecoms regulator acts as its data protection authority; no ruling against an organisation or published figures are known.
CIV.summary:
Named in law and appointed. Law No. 2013-450 of 19 June 2013 governs personal data protection, and a decree of 4 February 2015 names ARTCI as the body that receives declarations and imposes withdrawals and fines under it, with authorisation requests ruled on within one month. A 2022 fact sheet says a data protection authority is appointed, with 7 members serving up to 6 years. On 3 August 2026 ARTCI, styling itself the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles, issued a communique inviting controllers to use CERTINUM.

Rulings and published figures. The nearest held fact is the power the 2015 decree gives ARTCI: to rule on authorisation requests within one month and to impose withdrawals and fines. In its 3 August 2026 communique ARTCI says it launched CERTINUM on 2 July 2026.
